To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the genetic component of susceptibility to lung cancer is greater than previously estimated; and that (2) the genetic component is a function of the effects of smoking.

(i) the genetic component of familial aggregation of lung cancer is greater than previously estimated, (ii) the genetic component is greater for families of younger probands, and (iii) the genetic component may be due to susceptibility to the effects (or to the effects of a cofactor) of tobacco smoking.

(1) a Mendelian codominance model provides a good fit to lung cancer data from a large number of families, (2) the genetic component of risk is higher in younger families than in older families, (3) the genetic component is higher in families with parents who are more likely to have smoked than in families with parents less likely, and (4) the genetic component increases with pack‐years of smoking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the genetic and environmental causes of lung cancer.
identifying the genetic component of susceptibility to lung cancer.
the genetic and environmental factors which influence the development of lung cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present study are not conclusive.
the genetic component to lung cancer is not yet known, but is probably greater than previously estimated.
the genetic component in the etiology of lung cancer has been underestimated in previous studies, but that the magnitude of this genetic contribution is not yet established.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there is a genetic susceptibility to tobacco‐induced lung cancer that is inherited as an allele that produces an earlier age of cancer onset, and that the magnitude of this genetic component is influenced by cohort effects.

there are two types of lung cancer, one that is strongly influenced by smoking and one that is not, and that there are two major types of smokers: those with a genetic susceptibility to the carcinogenic effects of tobacco and those without.
the genetic component to the development of lung cancer is greater than previously estimated, and that susceptibility to lung disease is a function of susceptibility for the effects of tobacco smoke.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are cohort effects that can confound the results from genetic analyses.

the genetics of smoking‐related disease is not simple, and that it is important to understand the environmental factors that are involved in disease etiology, as well as to understand the genetic factors.
cohort differences in smoking habits may confound parameters of segregation analysis.
